Would Democracy work if you could vote against a presidential candidate?

It would work just about the same, but instead of voting for the person you want, you would vote for the person you don't. Honestly for the last several elections I would have much preferred voting against who I don't want, rather than just voting for the other person that I don't really like either.

It depends on how one defines "work."

If the system included a requirement for a minimum percentage of the total vote in order to win an election, it'd at least likely be somewhat less oppressive, since parties would have to run candidates who are actually attractive to voters, rather than being able to just get by with running the arguably least overtly destructive candidates. Genuinely noxious candidates would receive so many votes against them that it would be for all intents and purposes impossible for them to win an election, and an election between two essentially equally noxious candidates (the giant douche and the shit sandwich) could not produce a winner.

However, in the end, it would still suffer the more fundamental problem of democracy - the presumption that the will of a greater number of people is rightly imposed upon a lesser number of people, which presumption cannot ever really serve freedom.

...the will of a greater number of people is rightly imposed upon a lesser number of people...

I don't know why democracy is held up as the ultimate goal.

Broadly, it's because people tend to be irrationally self-involved, but can't bring themselves to consider that fact.

First - most people really don't fully grasp the fact that the other people with whom they share this planet are actual, full-fledged people. It's a thing they understand, to the extent they do, only intellectually. They can maybe reason through to the conclusion that all those other people are actual people, just like them, but they generally can't make it all the way to understanding that their internal lives are just as rich - that not only are they just as filled with hopes and dreams and fears and doubts and desires and goals, but that they're just as firmly attached to them. People tend to treat whatever it is that they value as that which necessarily possesses value, and whatever it is that someone else might value as somehow not even quite real. Yet they also tend to insist, and apparently actually believe, that they sympathize and empathize with and have respect for other people.

That's a mental trap. They generally fail to fully grasp the humanness of the people around them, but they do intellectually recognize it, and at least pay lip service to respecting it. So they're trapped between a fundamental disregard for the desires of others and a need to at least give the appearance of regard for those desires. That's why most oppose totalitarianism - it's not, as they'd prefer to believe, because of any real respect for the liberty of others, since they have no real respect for that - they can't even fully comprehend that those others really exist, much less that they have values that they wish to pursue, and much less yet that they have exactly as much of a right to pursue them. It's just that, once they've made the assertion that others deserve liberty, they can't rationally overtly call for the usurpation of that liberty. That sort of blatant contradiction would cast too harsh a light on their irrationality, and they simply can't tolerate that. And I don't think that's an external thing, but an internal one - it's not that the hypocrisy would diminish them in the eyes of others, but that it would undermine their own conception of themselves.

So they look for something external to themselves to take the responsibility, and as appropriate, the blame. Instead of overtly and directly seeking the imposition of their wills upon others and having to face the fact that they have no real regard for other people, they seek to align themselves with some third party that will carry out the imposition on their behalves. All the better if they can come together into some collective - that moves them even further from the appearance of responsibility for the oppression of another, since, after all, they're not doing it. They just got together with a bunch of other people and supported the establishment of some remote mechanism, and it did all the dirty work, while their hands remain clean. Their wills get imposed on other people, which is what they want, but it's all comfortably distant from them, so they can continue to pretend that they're advocates of liberty and lovers of humanity.

Thus, democracy. Democracy allows those who really couldn't care less about other people or their values to band together, and thus to spread the potential fault for the oppression of others as broadly and thinly as possible. I don't have to put a gun to someone else's head and force him to abide by my will - I can band together with a bunch of other people and designate some third party to go do all that messy and ugly oppressing somewhere well out of my sight, so I don't have to even consider the inherent contradiction between my purported support for liberty and the oppression that's carried out at my behest.

The curious thing that comes of that though is the situations in which the mob rules against the supporter of democracy. In many (most?) cases, the same people who would vote in support of the negation of the wills of others without even a moment's hesitation will suddenly rise up in self-righteous furor when it's their wills that are being negated. It's the exact same process by which they excuse whatever it is that they do to others, but as soon as it's others doing it to them, it's suddenly vile and reprehensible. Why? Because it's only then - only when it's no longer a distant and vague thing being done to one of those half-formed, shadowy beings that sort of hover around in the background of their lives that the truth of what it actually is becomes apparent.

Of course, next week, when the next vote goes their way again, they'll completely fail to make the connection, and they'll be right back to complete and total disregard for those shadowy and meaningless creatures whose wills are nominally rightly being negated.

And 'round and 'round it goes...

So as you said, Steampunk takes Victorian technology and aesthetics and creates a world of technology equivalent to ours. There's a few much less popular subgenres of steampunk that do similar things with different eras: Dieselpunk uses more of a '20s art deco vibe, and oilpunk can be seen in the game Dishonored.

Cyberpunk is the dystopian future as through the lens of the 1980s. It's film noir meets Atari 2600. Tron as done by EA. Everything is wet, dark, and dank, but there's a light, and it's neon. Wealth inequality to the extreme, you're either one of the elites in the white light of polished Apple Store sterility, or one of the dirty street rats scrounging to get by in the overcrowded megaplexes. It's Vegas at its most sinful with the population density of a coffin hotel.

If you don't know Gibson then you really are new to this. Here's a quick crash course on the two major subgenres of cyberpunk:

Classic cyberpunk was invented by William Gibson (although he mainly writes speculative fiction nowadays). Classic cyberpunk features antiheroes in gritty, edgy dystopian settings. The aesthetic was heavily inspired by film noir. William Gibson's Neuromancer is the biggest success from this school of cyberpunk. It seems to have died around the same time punk died in the 80s, for similar reasons. When I was in middle school in the 90s almost all the people on the alt.cyberpunk newsgroup said cyberpunk is dead.

Neocyberpunk was invented by Neal Stephenson (although he mainly writes historical fiction nowadays). Neocyberpunk features classic, virtuous heroes in settings that are gritty, but less noir-inspired than classic cyberpunk. Neocyberpunk follows a more traditional monomyth style of storytelling. Neal Stephenson's Snow Crash is the novel that kickstarted this subgenre. Diamond Age is another good example.

Today, classic and neo cyberpunk kind of blend a bit. The line isn't as distinct as it once was, but if you want to read the classics then these are the two subgenres you are going to be concerned with.

Of course, nowadays we have steam punk and pirate punk and diesel punk and hello kitty punk and whatever else the kids are on about. Some of that stuff is entertaining, but if you are a purist, these are really the two major branches of cyberpunk that have the most history and have had the most major influence on culture.
